h1:
Sticky Rice & Local Sweets
Saraburi — A Market Food Walk
intro: Saraburi is one of those towns where the old sweets have stuck around. You'll find coconut-glazed sticky rice (khao niao mun) with all kinds of toppings at morning markets, alongside rare Tai Yuan treats like khanom kong and khao kaeb that are getting harder to find every year. We walked markets in town and over in Sao Hai to pick 9 things worth your time — and tell you exactly which market, which day.

blocks.html: Most people think of Sao Hai curry puffs when they hear Saraburi food. But the local sweet scene runs much deeper than that. Saraburi is home to a Tai Yuan community — descendants of people who migrated from Chiang Saen and Chiang Rai in the early Rattanakosin era, settling around Sao Hai district. That history brought a set of sweets you won't find anywhere else in the region, sitting alongside the Central Thai-style khao niao mun sold at town markets every morning. So we split this into two tracks: the sticky rice toppings trail in town, and the Tai Yuan heritage sweets across the river in Sao Hai.

blocks.text: Khao Niao Mun Toppings You Should Try

blocks.html: Khao niao mun is glutinous rice steamed and folded with coconut milk and sugar until fragrant and rich, then served with a topping ("na") of your choice. At Saraburi's town markets, vendors scoop it into takeaway boxes and let you pick your topping. Here are the ones people order most — and the ones worth trying first.

items.name: Mango Sticky Rice (Khao Niao Mamuang)
items.blurb: The summer classic. Coconut-glazed sticky rice topped with sliced ripe mango — usually nam dok mai for its dense, floral sweetness, with ok rong as an alternative at some stalls. A drizzle of salted coconut cream cuts through the richness, finished with toasted mung beans. This is the one people queue for from March through May.

items.name: Sangkaya (Pandan Custard) Sticky Rice
items.blurb: Sticky rice with a smooth steamed pandan-egg custard on top. Gentler sweetness than the mango version, available year-round. Vendors who make their own custard get a distinct pandan fragrance and a clean sweetness — not the sharp, sugary kind. Second best-seller after mango.

items.name: Shrimp or Dried Fish Topping
items.blurb: For people who want savory-sweet rather than pure sweet. The topping is shrimp or minced dried fish stir-fried with palm sugar until fluffy and slightly caramelized, scattered over the coconut rice. Sweet-forward with a salty finish — more interesting than it sounds. A heritage topping that's slowly disappearing from regular markets.

items.name: Moo Yong (Shredded Pork) Sticky Rice
items.blurb: The one kids always go for. Lightly salted coconut rice topped with fluffy shredded pork — some stalls add Chinese sausage or goon chiang. Good as a quick morning bite before heading out. Easy to find on carts parked outside the market.

items.name: Tri-color Sliced Sticky Rice (Khao Niao Mun Tat)
items.blurb: Coconut sticky rice cut into bite-sized pieces, usually in three colors: white, pandan green, and butterfly pea purple. Sold alongside other toppings or packaged as a set. Holds well for several hours without losing texture — makes a good take-home gift from older rice sweet shops that have been doing this for decades.

blocks.title: Buying tips
blocks.html: Good khao niao mun should have coconut milk that coats the rice — rich, not watery. Check that the grains hold their shape without being soggy. Buy in the morning to get that day's freshly steamed batch. If you're ordering with mango, ask the vendor to pack the coconut cream drizzle separately so it doesn't go soft on the way home.

blocks.text: Tai Yuan Heritage Sweets — Getting Rarer Every Year

blocks.html: These are what make Saraburi different from other provinces. Several Tai Yuan sweets have fewer and fewer people making them. Most are found on the Sao Hai side of the river, particularly at Ban Ton Tan floating market — open Sundays only — where vendors dressed in traditional sarongs sell both savory and sweet dishes the old way.

items.name: Khanom Kong (Wagon Wheel Sweet)
items.blurb: An ancient sweet shaped like a wagon wheel, made from mung bean flour and palm sugar pressed into a ring, battered and deep-fried until the outside is crisp and the inside stays soft. Locals joke that coming to Saraburi without eating khanom kong is like not really showing up. It was traditionally made for merit-making ceremonies and weddings in Tai Yuan communities.

items.name: Khao Kaeb (Rice Sheets)
items.blurb: Thin rice flour sheets, similar in form to kite-shaped rice crackers, spread on cloth and sun-dried. Eaten fresh — soft and slightly chewy with nam phrik (chili dip) — or grilled and toasted until crisp, sprinkled with sesame. Every step is handmade. Find them at Ban Ton Tan floating market.

items.name: Khai Pam (Grilled Banana Leaf Egg)
items.blurb: Egg mixed with flour and spring onion, poured into a small banana leaf cup and grilled over charcoal until fragrant. Think fluffy omelette with a faint smoky-banana leaf scent. Eat straight off the grill while hot. A morning staple still sold at older local markets.

items.name: Paeng Ji (Griddled Rice Cakes)
items.blurb: Glutinous rice flour mixed with coconut and palm sugar, pressed flat and cooked on a griddle until golden and fragrant. Sweet, rich, soft and slightly chewy. A simple, homey sweet that Ban Ton Tan market still has to taste.

blocks.title: Timing tip
blocks.html: Most Tai Yuan sweets are made fresh and sell out fast. If you're tracking down khanom kong and khao kaeb at Ban Ton Tan market, aim to arrive by late morning — before noon. By mid-afternoon, the best items are usually gone.

blocks.text: Where to Actually Find These Sweets

blocks.html: Saraburi's local sweets aren't all in one place. Town markets cover the khao niao mun toppings; Sao Hai covers the Tai Yuan heritage sweets. Here's where to start.

items.name: Ban Ton Tan Ancient Floating Market (Sao Hai)
items.blurb: A Tai Yuan-style riverside market along the Pa Sak River. Open Sundays only, 08:00–16:00. Carries khanom kong, khao kaeb, khai pam, paeng ji, mee jae, and a Lanna dance performance around midday. The best single spot for heritage sweets.

items.name: Saraburi Town Morning Market (Pak Priao)
items.blurb: The municipal fresh market in town. Stalls sell khao niao mun with all kinds of toppings, seasonal mango sticky rice, and Thai dessert carts. Open every morning — good for a quick bite before heading out.

items.name: Tai Yuan Folk Culture Center, Saraburi
items.blurb: Not a market, but also on the Sao Hai side. A traditional Thai house museum telling the Tai Yuan story. Worth a stop before heading to the floating market — it adds context to the khanom kong and khao kaeb you're about to eat.

blocks.html: To cover both tracks in one trip, go on a Sunday — Ban Ton Tan market only opens that day. Do Sao Hai first while the heritage sweets are fully stocked, then loop back into town for sticky rice.

faq.q: What local sweets should I try in Saraburi?
faq.a: In town, go for mango sticky rice and pandan custard (sangkaya) sticky rice. For rare Tai Yuan heritage sweets that you won't find easily elsewhere, try khanom kong, khao kaeb, khai pam, and paeng ji. Locals say khanom kong is the one you can't leave without tasting.

faq.q: Where can I find traditional Thai sweets in Saraburi?
faq.a: Tai Yuan sweets like khanom kong and khao kaeb are concentrated at Ban Ton Tan Ancient Floating Market in Sao Hai district — open Sundays only, 08:00–16:00. For khao niao mun with various toppings, the morning market in Saraburi town has stalls open daily.

faq.q: What days is Ban Ton Tan market open?
faq.a: Sundays only, roughly 08:00 to 16:00, along the Pa Sak River in Ton Tan Subdistrict, Sao Hai. Aim to arrive before noon — many handmade items sell out well before closing time.

faq.q: When is the best time to eat mango sticky rice in Saraburi?
faq.a: March to May, when nam dok mai and ok rong mangoes are in season. The mangoes are sweeter, more fragrant, and better priced during this window. Sangkaya and other toppings are available year-round.

faq.q: What is khanom kong and why is it famous in Saraburi?
faq.a: Khanom kong is an ancient sweet shaped like a wagon wheel — mung bean flour and palm sugar formed into a ring, battered and deep-fried. It was traditionally made for merit ceremonies and auspicious events in Tai Yuan culture, giving it a long tie to Sao Hai's identity. That heritage is why it's become the town's signature sweet.
